summary: For ages 9–11, build understanding of glaciers and ice sheets across three linked processes: (1) FORMATION — snow accumulates over centuries and compresses through firn into dense glacial ice; (2) FLOW & SCULPTING — ice deforms and moves slowly downhill under its own weight, carving U-shaped valleys and depositing moraines; (3) ICE CORES as a climate ARCHIVE — trapped air bubbles at each depth are samples of ancient atmosphere, and because newer snow buries older layers, deeper ice is older, giving a record back ~800,000 years in the deepest Antarctic cores. Emphasise the long timescales (centuries to form, millennia recorded) and the idea that ice cores are decoded evidence, not just frozen water. Learners should run and decode these processes, not only recognise labelled parts.
misconceptions: Glaciers are frozen still and never move — they flow slowly downhill under their own weight
Glaciers form quickly from a cold winter — they build over centuries as snow compresses into ice
U-shaped valleys and scattered boulders are random — they are carved and dropped by past glaciers
Ice cores are just frozen water — their trapped air bubbles are samples of ancient atmosphere, a climate archive
Shallow and deep ice are the same age — deeper ice is older, recording further back in time

activities.title: Run a glacier from snowfall to sculpted valley
steps: Pile successive snowfalls onto a mountain and advance a time slider through centuries, watching flakes crush into firn and then into dense blue glacial ice.
Release the glacier and observe it creep downhill very slowly, like slow treacle, grinding a rounded U-shaped valley.
Watch the glacier drop a ridge of rock (a moraine) at its snout, and identify where erosion and where deposition happen.
Describe in your own words why the solid ice moves at all (its own great weight plus gravity cause it to deform and flow).

Predict and then test: what happens if melting at the glacier's lower end (its snout) outpaces new snowfall at the top? (The ice still flows downhill, but the snout retreats uphill as the glacier shrinks.)
activities.insight: A glacier is solid but not static: it is fed by compressed snow at the top and flows downhill under gravity, shaping the land by eroding valleys and depositing moraines over very long timescales.

activities.title: Drill and decode an ice core
steps: Lower a drill into an ice sheet and pull up a core showing dated layers.
Tap air bubbles trapped at different depths and watch a climate graph plot backward in time as each bubble's data is added.
State which bubbles are recent air and which are oldest, and explain the rule: deeper ice is older.
Follow the record to near the bottom and read how far back it reaches (~800,000 years in the deepest Antarctic cores).
Explain in a sentence or two how a scientist could read the climate of 100,000 years ago from a stick of ice.
activities.insight: Ice cores are a climate archive: each trapped air bubble is a sample of the atmosphere from around when that layer sealed, and because layers accumulate over time, deeper ice records further back.

activities.title: Read glacial action from real landscapes
steps: Examine photographs or diagrams of U-shaped valleys, scattered erratic boulders, and moraine ridges.
For each feature, explain what past glacial process (erosion by flowing ice, or deposition of carried rock) created it.
Contrast a U-shaped glacial valley with a V-shaped river valley and say what the shape tells you about how it formed.
Explain why scattered boulders far from any cliff, especially ones made of a different rock from the ground beneath them, can be evidence that ice carried them there in the past.
activities.insight: Present-day landforms are evidence of past glacial action: shapes and deposits let us read where ice flowed, eroded, and dropped its load.

activities.title: Sequence and ordering check
steps: Put the formation stages in order: snowflakes → firn → dense glacial ice.
Order a set of ice-core layers from youngest to oldest and justify the ordering by depth.
Answer: if all the ice in Antarctica's ice sheet melted, roughly what would happen to sea level, and why would it be so much?
activities.insight: Consolidate the formation sequence, the depth-to-age rule, and the scale of water stored in the ice sheets.

activities.title: Talk it through with an ice-core scientist
steps: Through a spoken or role-play exchange, ask how a core is drilled and what the layers and bubbles mean.
Respond to the prompt 'how can something solid flow?' by explaining accumulation plus gravity-driven deformation.
Pose and answer: if the mountain were perfectly flat with no slope, would the ice still flow, and why or why not?
activities.insight: Articulating the processes aloud in a responsive exchange reinforces causal reasoning about flow, formation, and the ice-core record.

checkQuestion: A glacier looks like a solid, still block of ice sitting on a mountain. But scientists say a glacier 'flows' like a very slow river. How can something solid flow, and where does all that ice come from in the first place? Tell me, and then tell me WHY it moves instead of just staying put.
checkAnswer: Snow piles up year after year and its weight compresses the lower layers into dense glacier ice. Because the mass is so heavy, gravity makes the whole thing slowly deform and slide downhill — it flows like an extremely slow river, carving valleys as it goes. So a glacier is solid but not static: it is fed by snow at the top and flows and melts away at the bottom.
